Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic translation require initiator codon (AUG) as a start signal. However, only prokaryotic translation requires additional start signal called Shine-Dalgarno sequence to ensure that multiple protein products can be synthesised from polygenic mRNA. In eukaryotes, the 5' end of mRNA is capped and the 3' end is polyadenylated. This means that there is no need for Shine-Dalgarno sequence because each mRNA will code for one single protein product. Therefore, it is not possible to have multiple proteins being translated at the same time. Hence, prokaryotic translation requires this additional start signal to allow multiple protein products to be produced.  Reference: Lecture slides - Unit 2, slide 18; and Unit 4, slide 6. This statement is false because while it is true that the 5' cap functions as a docking site for the initiation complex and is therefore essential in translation, it is not true that mRNA with no 5' cap cannot be translated. Internal ribosome entry sites (IRES) are regions of mRNA that recruit the ribosome to initiate translation without the need for a 5' cap. Therefore, IRESs allow for mRNA to be translated even when they do not have a 5' cap. The second part of this statement is also untrue because some mRNAs have both a 5' cap and an internal ribosome entry site. These mRNAs have two potential start codons so that they can be translated by different mechanisms: cap-dependent and cap-independent. This allows them to be translated under different conditions. For example, viral mRNA has both a 5' cap and an internal ribosome entry site. Under normal conditions, the 5' cap is used as the start codon and the mRNA is translated normally. However, during viral infection, the host cell may produce factors which degrade the 5' cap. When this happens, the internal ribosome entry site is able to recruit the ribosome and translate the mRNA. The reverse can also occur, whereby the 5' cap is intact but the internal ribosome entry site is damaged. In this case, the mRNA would only be translated using the 5' cap. Thus, it is possible for mRNA to have both a 5' cap and an internal ribosome entry site. I hope this explanation helps clarify why this statement is false! A is false because plasmids do not need to be linked to chromosomal replication. D is false because plasmids can be excised from the chromosome using only one endonuclease. Plasmids are not required to have the same Ori sequence as the rest of the chromosome, nor do they require two different enzymes to be cut from the parent DNA. Plasmids may contain coding sequences that are not essential for the functioning of the cell, but rather provide an advantage in certain circumstances. They may also contain non-coding sequences that serve no known purpose. In either case, it is likely that these sequences will remain in place even if they are not needed at any given time. This means that there is no reason why a plasmid should ever become non-functional due to mutations affecting its coding ability. Instead, such mutations would simply result in loss of function for those parts of the plasmid which rely on them. As long as there remains some functional sequence left over, then there will still be something useful about this part of the plasmid. For example, suppose we had a plasmid containing a gene encoding a protein involved in metabolism. If we were able to identify all possible mutations that could prevent expression of this protein, then we might expect that none of them would affect other genes within our plasmid. However, if instead we discovered that some mutations did affect other genes, then we would know that those particular regions of the plasmid were not essential for its survival and so could safely be removed without affecting anything else. We would also learn that those parts of the plasmid which remained intact were still useful even though they weren't absolutely necessary

The process of polyadenylation occurs after transcription has been completed. Poly(A) is not involved in transcription but rather in translation. The presence of a poly(A) tail does not contribute towards mRNA stability, but instead contributes towards the translation efficiency of mRNA. The poly(A) tail also promotes the export of mRNA out of the nucleus. It is important that we understand that there are two separate processes taking place here: transcription and translation. The poly(A) tail is only associated with the latter process - translation. And finally, it should be noted that the process of polyadenylation is not always accurate, as sometimes the poly(A) tail may be missing completely or there may be more than one poly(A) tail present.
